title: Two quasars heated a vast bubble in the young universe
freshness: Peer-reviewed Nature Astronomy article published November 18, 2026; preferred 15-day search window.
excerpt: Millimeter observations have revealed an immense store of hot gas around two quasars seen 2.8 billion years after the Big Bang. Its measured thermal energy is far greater than gravity alone is expected to produce, pointing to powerful heating by growing black holes.
whyItMatters: Galaxy models rely on energy from feeding black holes to slow or stop star formation, but the hottest gas is difficult to measure directly. This result weighs that hidden energy around an individual early quasar system and finds enough to reshape its large-scale environment.
whatToExploreNext: How does the thermal Sunyaev-Zel'dovich effect turn a small dip in millimeter light into a measurement of hot gas pressure and energy?

sources.label: Excess intergalactic heating around a dual quasar system 2.8 Gyr after the Big Bang

body:
## A pressure shadow around two quasars

Two feeding supermassive black holes appear to have heated an enormous reservoir of gas when the universe was only about 2.8 billion years old. Astronomers found the gas around J1549+1245, a pair of quasar-hosting galaxies separated by roughly 19 kiloparsecs. A quasar is the intensely bright center of a galaxy where matter falling toward a black hole releases energy.

The gas is too hot and thin to map easily through ordinary X-rays. Instead, the team measured its effect on the cosmic microwave background, the faint afterglow of the early universe. When those background photons pass through very hot electrons, collisions shift some of their energy. At millimeter wavelengths, that shift appears as a small deficit of light called the thermal Sunyaev-Zel'dovich effect, or tSZ effect.

This deficit acts like a pressure shadow. Its strength measures the total electron pressure in the gas, allowing astronomers to estimate thermal energy without first knowing the gas density and temperature separately.

## Measuring the hidden heat

The researchers combined observations from the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array, its compact array, the Very Large Array, and the Submillimeter Array. They modeled emission from dust, star formation, and the active galactic centers across frequencies from radio to the near-infrared. What remained around the fainter member of the pair was a millimeter dip matching the spectral shape expected from the tSZ effect.

The localized signal was detected at six standard deviations, a statistical measure indicating that random noise is an unlikely explanation. It traces hot gas across at least 10 to 15 kiloparsecs and corresponds to a thermal energy of about 9.7 × 10^60 ergs, with an uncertainty of 1.6 × 10^60 ergs. That is 3.6 times the energy expected from all the hot gas in a dark matter halo weighing 10 trillion Suns. Gravity heating gas as it falls into the halo therefore cannot readily account for the full measurement.

The interferometer data also show a separate, broader decrement about 100 kiloparsecs across at five standard deviations. Some sensitivity extends to scales near 600 kiloparsecs. This wider feature is evidence for additional hot gas, though its exact origin is less certain than the localized detection.

## Observed energy, inferred cause

The millimeter deficit and its energy are measurements. The conclusion that quasar-driven winds supplied the excess heat is an interpretation based on the energy budget, the location of the gas, and comparisons with simulations. The two quasars are powerful enough to provide it. Under an assumed active lifetime of 100 million years, at least 0.6 percent of their lifetime energy output would need to couple to the surrounding gas.

That percentage sounds small, but the resulting heat is large enough in the authors' models to suppress star formation and warm gas beyond the host galaxies. A quasar can therefore affect more than the material immediately around its black hole. It can influence whether nearby gas cools into future stars.

This process is called black-hole feedback. Simulations use it to prevent massive galaxies from forming too many stars, yet direct measurements of its hottest phase have been scarce, especially in individual systems so early in cosmic history. J1549+1245 provides an unusually concrete energy account: a measured reservoir of hot gas, an excess beyond halo heating, and two active black holes capable of supplying it.
